items.prompt: Which property most directly justifies binary search?

options.text: The input contains many elements.
After evaluating a midpoint, one side can be proven unable to contain the answer.
The values are numeric.
The implementation uses a variable named mid.

feedback.reason: Binary search is legal only when midpoint information proves that an entire region can be discarded.

blocks.text: Binary search maintains an active ordered candidate interval that is known to contain every still-possible answer. A midpoint observation is useful only when the problem's order or predicate proves that one whole side cannot contain the required answer. Removing that side preserves the invariant and reduces the candidate count; input size, numeric type, and variable names provide no such proof.

blocks.title: Required proof sentence
blocks.text: Define exactly what mid tests, which region each result eliminates, and why every answer in that region is impossible. If either branch lacks that sentence, ordinary binary search is not justified.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.large_input: Large input creates a performance need, not a correctness rule.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.numeric_values: Binary search can work on non-numeric ordered domains, and numbers alone do not create a discard rule.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_variable: A midpoint variable does not prove correctness or logarithmic progress.

items.prompt: A sorted array is searched for a value using an arbitrary predicate that can be true, then false, then true again. Is binary search justified by sorted input alone?

options.text: Yes. Sorted values always make every predicate binary-searchable.
Yes, as long as a midpoint is inspected.
No. The predicate does not define one discardable boundary.
Yes, when the array is large enough.

feedback.reason: Sorted input is not sufficient when the searched property lacks monotonic structure.

blocks.text: Sorting orders the stored values, but binary search must eliminate candidates according to the property being queried. If that predicate can be true, then false, then true again, observing true or false at mid does not determine the predicate on either complete side. Discarding a half could remove a later valid answer.

blocks.title: One midpoint result gives no direction
blocks.text: For predicate values [false, true, false, true], a false result at index 2 cannot discard the left side because index 1 is true, and it cannot discard the right side because index 3 is true. The searched property has no single boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_sorted: Sorting the values does not make an unrelated predicate monotonic.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_mid: Inspecting a midpoint is only a sampling action; without monotonicity, its result cannot eliminate either complete side.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_large: A larger input increases the cost of a scan but does not turn a multi-transition predicate into one searchable boundary.

items.prompt: Which task has a clear binary-search signal?

options.text: Count the frequency of each character in a string.
Generate every permutation of n values.
Compute all prefix sums.
Find the first integer x for which a monotonic predicate feasible(x) becomes true.

feedback.reason: A monotonic false-to-true transition creates a searchable boundary.

blocks.text: A false-to-true predicate partitions an ordered domain into a false prefix and a true suffix. The required answer is the boundary between them, so evaluating the midpoint gives directional evidence.

items: If feasible(mid) is false, every candidate at or left of mid is false, so the first true must be to the right.
If feasible(mid) is true, mid is a candidate and every later value is also true, so candidates strictly right of mid cannot be the first true.
Continue until the interval isolates the smallest true candidate; explicitly handle the case where no true candidate exists.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.count_letters: Frequency accumulation does not halve a search domain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_permutations: Enumeration requires exploring many branches rather than discarding one half.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.running_sum: Each prefix sum depends on the preceding accumulated state; a midpoint result cannot replace the required left-to-right updates.

items.prompt: An unsorted array must be searched for one exact value, and no preprocessing is allowed. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Binary search is valid because exact equality can be checked at mid.
Binary search is not justified because comparisons at mid do not eliminate either side.
The algorithm may behave as though the input were sorted.
The parity of mid determines which side to discard.

feedback.reason: Without ordering or another monotonic structure, midpoint comparison does not provide directional evidence.

blocks.text: Equality at mid can finish an exact search, but a mismatch in an unsorted array says nothing about target location. A smaller target may be on either side, and so may a larger target. With preprocessing forbidden, every uninspected position remains possible and a linear scan is the direct correct strategy.

blocks.title: The same midpoint supports opposite directions
blocks.text: In [1, 9, 4], inspecting middle value 9 while searching for 1 requires going left. In [4, 9, 1] the identical midpoint comparison requires going right. The midpoint result alone cannot choose safely.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_anyway: A mismatch at mid gives no direction in an unsorted array.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_implicitly: Treating the array as sorted invents an order the input does not satisfy, so comparison direction can discard the actual target.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.use_mid_parity: Even and odd indices have no stated relationship to target location, so parity cannot prove either side impossible.

items.prompt: A problem asks for the smallest capacity that can process all jobs within a deadline, and larger capacities never make the schedule worse. What is the binary-search signal?

options.text: The jobs can be sorted.
Capacity is numeric.
Feasibility changes monotonically from false to true as capacity increases.
The deadline value is large.

feedback.reason: The answer domain has a first feasible capacity.

blocks.text: Because increasing capacity never makes the schedule worse, capacities form a false prefix followed by a true suffix under feasible(capacity). The optimization asks for the first true value, not merely any feasible one.

items: Test whether all jobs meet the deadline at capacity mid.
If infeasible, every smaller capacity is also infeasible, so discard capacities through mid.
If feasible, retain mid as a possible optimum and discard larger candidates that cannot be the minimum.
The surviving boundary is the smallest feasible capacity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.jobs_sorted: Sorting may help the predicate but does not define the answer boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.capacity_numeric: Numbers provide an order, but binary search additionally needs the stated fact that feasibility changes in only one direction over that order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.deadline_large: The deadline's magnitude affects feasibility values but does not itself prove that a midpoint result eliminates a capacity interval.

items.prompt: Which statement is an unsafe heuristic?

options.text: "A midpoint comparison proves one region cannot contain the answer."
"The predicate has one truth transition over an ordered domain."
"In a rotated array with distinct values, one half is still ordered."
"The input is sorted, so binary search must be the best choice."

feedback.reason: Sorted input is helpful only when the query and cost model make midpoint elimination legal and useful.

blocks.text: Sorted values support binary search only when the requested comparison aligns with that order. Exact lookup and lower-bound queries do; an unrelated non-monotonic property may not. Even when binary search is legal, 'best' also depends on preprocessing, access cost, query count, and whether the output must preserve original order.

blocks.title: Sorted is evidence, not a complete proof
blocks.text: Name the midpoint test and both legal discard branches. If the query does not let sorted order rule out an entire side, the array being sorted is only a surface similarity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.discard_rule: This is not an unsafe heuristic: it states the central proof obligation that makes a binary-search branch legal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.monotonic_boundary: One truth transition over an ordered domain is substantive structure from which first-true or last-true elimination follows.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ordered_half: With the distinct-value constraint, an ordered active half supports a concrete target-range test and a legal rotated-search branch.

items.prompt: Why does using left, right, and mid not by itself prove O(log n) time?

options.text: Variable names determine asymptotic complexity.
The active search interval must shrink by a constant factor and midpoint work must be bounded.
Any algorithm with three variables is logarithmic.
Integer indices always produce halving.

feedback.reason: Logarithmic iteration count comes from strict halving of the remaining domain.

blocks.text: If an interval of size n is reduced to at most about n/2 after every midpoint evaluation, after k iterations at most n/2^k candidates remain. Reaching one candidate requires k = Θ(log n). Names such as left, right, and mid do not establish that recurrence.

blocks.title: Iterations are not total cost
blocks.text: The interval updates must strictly exclude mid or otherwise prove progress. If one midpoint evaluation costs T(n), the search can cost Θ(T(n) log n), plus any preprocessing; logarithmic iteration count alone is not an O(log n) total-time proof.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_names: Renaming variables cannot change how much the interval shrinks or how much work one iteration performs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.three_variables: A constant number of variables bounds some storage, not iteration count; the updates could still shrink by one or fail to progress.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.integer_indices: Updates may fail to shrink or may move by one position.

items.prompt: A rotated sorted array contains distinct values. Why can binary search still be legal?

options.text: Rotation automatically disappears after choosing mid.
All values become equal after rotation.
At least one half of the active interval is ordered, allowing a target-range test.
The pivot is always given explicitly.

feedback.reason: Distinct-value rotation preserves enough local order to identify one sorted half.

blocks.text: A rotation creates one break in an otherwise ascending order. With distinct values, comparing the active left endpoint with mid identifies at least one ordered half; equality cannot hide which side is ordered.

items: Identify the ordered half of the current interval.
Test whether target lies inside that half's inclusive value range, accounting for whether mid was already checked.
If it does, retain that half; otherwise discard it and retain the other half.
Repeat on the smaller interval. The pivot need not be known in advance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rotation_removed: Choosing mid does not modify the array or remove its pivot; the algorithm succeeds by reasoning about one ordered half.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_values_equal: Rotation preserves every value, and the prompt explicitly says values are distinct; equality is neither created nor required.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.pivot_known: Rotated search can work without a known pivot.

items.prompt: A predicate over indices follows false, true, false, true. What is the correct diagnosis?

options.text: It is valid because a first true value exists.
It is valid because indices are ordered.
Choosing a different midpoint formula makes it monotonic.
It is not a valid single-boundary predicate for ordinary binary search.

feedback.reason: Ordinary boundary search needs one directional truth transition.

blocks.text: Having a first true index is not enough. First-true binary search requires every earlier value to be false and every value from the boundary onward to remain true. The sequence false, true, false, true crosses the boundary three times, so a midpoint result cannot characterize a complete side.

blocks.title: A first true can still be lost
blocks.text: At index 2 the predicate is false. Moving right because false supposedly means 'before the boundary' discards the actual first true at index 1. No midpoint formula can repair a non-monotonic predicate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_true_valid: Existence of a first true does not imply later values remain true.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_indices: An ordered domain is necessary but not sufficient.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_fixes: Floor- versus ceiling-biased midpoints can fix progress at adjacent boundaries, but neither can remove the predicate's multiple truth transitions.

items.prompt: A sorted array is queried once for whether any element satisfies an expensive non-monotonic condition. What should determine the strategy?

options.text: Binary search is always faster on sorted arrays.
Whether the condition supports a legal elimination rule, not merely that the values are sorted.
Sort the array again before searching.
Check only the midpoint and return its condition result.

feedback.reason: The query semantics determine whether sorted order is useful.

blocks.text: The existential query asks whether any element satisfies the expensive condition. If the condition is non-monotonic with respect to sorted value order, a false result at mid does not rule out satisfying values on either side, and a true result only supplies an early success. In the worst case every element may require evaluation; sorting again does not change the predicate.

blocks.title: The query must consume the order
blocks.text: Ask whether predicate(mid) implies anything about all candidates left or right of mid. If neither result safely eliminates a side, use a scan or a problem-specific index rather than sampling the midpoint.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_binary: Sorted storage makes value comparisons directional only for aligned queries; the stated expensive condition remains non-monotonic and supplies no legal branch.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_sort_again: The array is already sorted, and sorting does not make the predicate monotonic.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_sample: One sample cannot answer an existential query without structure.

items.prompt: Which problem most naturally supports searching for the last valid value?

options.text: Find any local maximum in an arbitrary unsorted sequence using the same rule for every input.
Count occurrences in an unsorted array without preprocessing.
Find the greatest threshold for which a monotonic feasibility predicate remains true.
Generate every subset.

feedback.reason: A true-to-false predicate over an ordered domain defines a last-true boundary.

blocks.text: A monotonic true-to-false predicate partitions the ordered thresholds into a valid prefix and an invalid suffix. The requested maximum feasible threshold is the last true value at that boundary.

items: If feasible(mid) is true, save mid as a candidate and search right for a larger valid threshold.
If feasible(mid) is false, every larger threshold is also false, so discard mid and the entire right side.
When the interval is exhausted, return the greatest saved true candidate or the contract's no-valid-value result.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.arbitrary_local_max: An arbitrary local-maximum landscape can rise and fall repeatedly, so the same midpoint result does not identify one discardable side on every input.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.count_occurrences_unsorted: Without preprocessing, any uninspected element can equal the target, and counting requires finding every occurrence rather than one boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.enumerate_subsets: The output requires all subsets, so discarding half of the candidate family would omit required results instead of preserving correctness.

items.prompt: When can repeated queries make preprocessing for binary search attractive?

options.text: For every single query regardless of preprocessing cost.
When original order must be preserved but indices are discarded.
When the query predicate remains non-monotonic after preprocessing.
When one preprocessing cost enables many later logarithmic queries and the order contract permits it.

feedback.reason: Strategy choice should include both preprocessing and query volume.

blocks.text: For n unsorted values and q exact-membership queries, repeated scans cost Θ(qn). Sorting a permitted copy once and then binary-searching costs Θ(n log n + q log n), plus Θ(n) copy space when source order must remain unchanged. Preprocessing is attractive only when that total workload and its state trade-off beat the legal alternative.

blocks.title: Amortization cannot waive semantics
blocks.text: Many queries can justify setup cost, but only if the ordered representation preserves required identity and order and the query itself has a legal discard rule. A non-monotonic predicate remains non-monotonic after an unrelated sort.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_query_always: A one-off sort can cost more than a scan.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.order_must_preserve: Discarding original indices while sorting prevents mapping a found value back to the required encounter order or source identity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.predicate_nonmonotonic: Preprocessing pays off only if it creates structure used by the query; a still-non-monotonic predicate has no single boundary to search.

items.prompt: Which components belong in a complete justification for ordinary monotonic-boundary binary search? Select all that apply.

options.text: The candidate domain has a total order.
The input is large, with no other structure.
Midpoint evidence proves an entire region cannot contain the answer.
A predicate changes truth value at most once in the searched direction.

feedback.reason: A complete boundary-search proof combines an ordered candidate domain, one truth transition, and a midpoint rule that safely discards a region.

blocks.text: The three accepted statements are jointly meaningful. The total order defines left and right, the single transition defines the desired boundary, and the discard proof connects predicate(mid) to the side that cannot contain that boundary. Omitting any one leaves an incomplete correctness argument.

blocks.title: Size is only motivation
blocks.text: A large domain may make logarithmic search desirable, but it does not create order, monotonicity, or a legal branch. Those properties must be proven independently.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.large_only: Size creates performance pressure but supplies none of the required order, single-transition, or midpoint-elimination facts.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.ordered_domain: The total order defines what left and right mean; without it, a directional boundary search has no candidate geometry.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.discard_proof: This connects each midpoint result to a region proven unable to contain the boundary, preserving correctness after deletion.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.single_transition: One truth transition partitions the domain into two uniform regions and makes first-true or last-true meaningful.

items.prompt: Which observations are insufficient by themselves to justify binary search? Select all that apply.

options.text: The data values are sorted.
The proposed code uses a midpoint variable.
The predicate is proven monotonic over an ordered finite domain.
The desired answer is numeric.

feedback.reason: Surface properties do not replace the half-discard proof.

blocks.text: Sorted values are insufficient when the query does not align with value order; a midpoint variable is only syntax; and a numeric answer can still have arbitrary feasibility. By contrast, a proven monotonic predicate over an ordered finite domain supplies a single truth boundary from which first-true or last-true discard rules can be derived.

blocks.title: Necessary is not sufficient
blocks.text: An ordered domain helps define direction but does not alone say what predicate(mid) means. State the transition and both discard branches before choosing binary search.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.monotonic_predicate: Unlike the surface clues, proven monotonicity over an ordered finite domain creates a single boundary and supports directional elimination.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_values: The queried property may vary non-monotonically despite value order, so sorting alone cannot determine a discard branch.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.uses_mid: A midpoint variable is syntax; it proves neither that one side is impossible nor that the next interval strictly shrinks.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.numeric_answer: Numbers are ordered, but their feasibility can still alternate many times, leaving no single searchable boundary.

items.prompt: Which tasks can legally use a binary-search family mechanism? Select all that apply.

options.text: Find an exact target in ascending sorted data.
Find a target in arbitrary unsorted data without preprocessing.
Find the first true value of a false-to-true monotonic predicate.
Find a target in a rotated sorted array with distinct values.

feedback.reason: Each accepted task has a specific invariant that supports directional elimination.

blocks.text: Exact lookup in ascending data uses value comparison to discard the impossible side. First-true search uses a false prefix and true suffix. Rotated distinct search identifies an ordered active half and tests target membership in its range. These are different invariants within the same elimination family.

blocks.title: Why arbitrary unsorted lookup is excluded
blocks.text: A mismatch at mid in unsorted data leaves the target possible on both sides. Without preprocessing, no directional elimination follows.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.arbitrary_unsorted: Without preprocessing, a midpoint mismatch leaves the target possible on both sides, so neither half can be discarded safely.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.exact_sorted: Ascending order makes target-versus-mid comparison prove the target, if present, can remain on only one side.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.first_true: The false-prefix/true-suffix transition lets a false mid discard left candidates and a true mid discard later non-first candidates.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.rotated_distinct: Distinctness lets the algorithm identify one ordered active half and test whether the target lies in its value range.

items.prompt: A binary search examines Θ(log W) candidate values, and one monotonic-predicate evaluation costs Θ(P(n)). Select the tightest offered total-time and iterative auxiliary-space bounds.
constraints: W is the size of the ordered candidate range.
Each predicate evaluation uses O(1) auxiliary space and releases it before returning.
The iterative search itself stores only a constant number of boundary variables.

feedback.reason: Binary search controls the number of predicate calls, not the internal cost of one call.

blocks.text: The search makes Θ(log W) predicate calls, each costing Θ(P(n)), so sequential work multiplies to Θ(P(n) log W), matching the offered O(P(n) log W) bound. The predicate and iterative search both use O(1) auxiliary space under the explicit constraints, and predicate-local storage is released between calls, so peak auxiliary space remains O(1).

blocks.title: Why the other offered bounds are wrong
blocks.text: Time O(log W) omits predicate cost, O(P(n)) omits repeated calls, and O(W·P(n)) is loose rather than tight. Space O(log W), O(P(n)), and O(W) contradict the stated iterative constant-state and constant-space predicate contracts.
